passages.text: VEINS, in mineralogy, are the clefts or fissures in rocks, filled with metallic ores, spar, quartz, or other matter different from the rock in which they lie. When rich in metal the miners call them lodes.

It was long the opinion of the ancients, and of the alchemists, that metals grow in the earth like plants, by the influence of the sun and planets; each metal being ruled by its own planet, as gold by the sun and silver by the moon.

Mr Werner of Freyberg holds that veins were at first open fissures, formed as the rocks dried and settled, and that they were afterwards filled from above by water, which deposited the ores and spars that it held in solution.
Dr Hutton, on the contrary, maintains that the matter of veins was forced up from below in a melted state, by the power of subterraneous heat.
Veins in the same district commonly run in one direction; and where two veins cross, the vein that is cut through is the older.
Many miners trust to the divining rod, a forked twig of hazel which, held in the hands, bends down over a vein; and some writers affirm that it seldom fails.

In geology, a vein is a distinct sheetlike body of crystallized minerals within a rock. Veins form when mineral constituents carried by an aqueous solution within the rock mass are deposited through precipitation.
The fluids that deposit veins are usually hot water solutions, called hydrothermal fluids, which move through cracks in the rock and drop minerals as they cool or as pressure falls.
Most veins form in fractures that open when the rock is under stress, and the minerals often grow from the walls of the crack inward.
Veins of quartz and other minerals can carry gold, silver, copper, tin and other metals, and many have been mined as lodes.
Veins in one area often share the same direction, because they fill fractures formed by the same regional stress.
Where one vein cuts across another, the vein that is cut is older.
Hydrothermal fluids are often released from cooling bodies of magma deep below, and rise through the crust.

reasons: The old headword VEINS, in mineralogy, maps to the geological sense of vein.
Rare terms appear in both: fissures, ores, quartz, lodes.
Ore genesis scores well but covers all ore deposits, not only veins.

alignments.label: Filled fissures

britannica.quote: the clefts or fissures in rocks, filled with metallic ores, spar, quartz

wikipedia.quote: a distinct sheetlike body of crystallized minerals within a rock

alignments.note: Same object in new words. Both describe a sheet of minerals that fills a crack in rock.

alignments.label: Metals grow

britannica.quote: metals grow in the earth like plants, by the influence of the sun and planets

wikipedia.quote: carried by an aqueous solution within the rock mass are deposited through precipitation

alignments.note: The 1797 entry reports this as an old belief. Metals do not grow. Water carries them and deposits them.

alignments.label: Filled by water

britannica.quote: filled from above by water, which deposited the ores and spars

wikipedia.quote: usually hot water solutions, called hydrothermal fluids

alignments.note: Werner was right that water deposits the minerals. The water is usually hot and rises from below, not from above.

alignments.label: Rocks dried and settled

britannica.quote: formed as the rocks dried and settled

wikipedia.quote: Most veins form in fractures that open when the rock is under stress

alignments.note: Change in knowledge. The cracks come from stress in the crust, not from rocks drying after a primeval ocean.

alignments.label: Melted matter from below

britannica.quote: forced up from below in a melted state

wikipedia.quote: Hydrothermal fluids are often released from cooling bodies of magma deep below

alignments.note: Hutton was right about heat and a source below. Most veins form from hot water, which often comes from magma, not from melted vein matter.

alignments.label: One direction

britannica.quote: Veins in the same district commonly run in one direction

wikipedia.quote: Veins in one area often share the same direction

alignments.note: Same observation. Wikipedia gives the cause: the same regional stress.

alignments.label: Older vein is cut

britannica.quote: the vein that is cut through is the older

wikipedia.quote: Where one vein cuts across another, the vein that is cut is older

alignments.note: The rule holds and is still used to date veins.

alignments.label: Divining rod

britannica.quote: Many miners trust to the divining rod

alignments.note: Wikipedia's vein article does not mention it. Inference from other sources: dowsing has failed controlled tests and does not find veins.

alignments.label: Growth from the walls

wikipedia.quote: the minerals often grow from the walls of the crack inward

alignments.note: New detail. The 1797 entry does not say how the crystals grow in the fissure.

suggestedQuestions: Who was right about veins, Werner or Hutton?
Did people think metals grow in the earth?
Which 1797 claims about veins still hold?

Who was right about veins, Werner or Hut.answer: Each was partly right. Werner said water filled the veins from above [B3]. Hutton said melted matter came up from below [B4]. Wikipedia says hot water solutions deposit the minerals [W2], and these fluids often come from magma deep below [W7].

Did people think metals grow in the eart.answer: Yes. The 1797 entry reports the old belief that metals grow like plants under the sun and planets [B2]. Wikipedia says the minerals are carried by water and deposited [W1].

Which 1797 claims about veins still hold.answer: The field rules hold. Veins in one district run in one direction [B5] [W5], and a vein that is cut is older [B5] [W6]. The divining rod [B6] and growing metals [B2] do not.
